text:
Direct recurrent precedents exist. [Tan et al. (2016)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1606.08117) train GRUs on every session prefix, each labeled with its immediately following item, and apply embedding dropout to generate pruned training inputs. Prefix expansion changes the supervised examples; it differs from removing an old prefix while retaining the same endpoint and next-item target. Standard [GRU4Rec](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf) already supervises successive next-item transitions. Thus, more training prefixes alone need not introduce new targets relative to an all-position baseline.

[CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/html/2010.14395) randomly retains a contiguous subsequence of length ⌊ηL⌋, or applies masking/reordering, to construct two views for contrastive learning alongside recommendation loss. These crops need not preserve the original endpoint; they provide representation-level supervision rather than automatically defining aligned next-item labels. CL4SRec is contrastive, not a Cloze masked-item reconstruction method. [Recency dropout](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11016) is another recurrent precedent, designed to counter excessive dependence on recent interactions; its motivation differs from discarding old context.

Assessment: cropping itself has clear precedents; the plausible contribution is the matched-supervision experiment, pending broader novelty checking. Compare random contiguous crops, endpoint-preserving suffixes, and input dropout while holding target identities, supervised positions, target weighting, optimizer updates, and inference history limits constant. For suffix x[s:t], preserve target x[t+1]; for all-position training, retain each position’s original next-item label and exclude removed positions from loss. Arbitrary interior crops require either their actual following item or an explicitly defined longer-horizon objective. Evaluate with all available history within the same fixed maximum length and dropout disabled. This isolates context removal from altered supervision or inference truncation.
